The thing that you have to remember is that international football represents the achievements of the national FA more than just a coach or a group of players. The rather annoying thing about this though is that changes you make now won't be seen in the full international team for a good 10 years or so, and of course if you don't do very well next year then there is widespread pressure to change something.

This has always been England's problem - we have made more structural changes in the grassroots and Academy side of the game than every major country in the world because we're idiots who are chasing our tails. Let's say we set up a new plan in 2000, expecting this to come to fruition in 2010. When we perform badly in 2004, the media and the fans go nuts and then SOMETHING MUST BE DONE about the state of grassroots so a whole new idea is tried meaning that the focus of the group that started in 2000 then becomes changed in 2004 and a new plan is drawn up. By 2010 they aren't the players envisaged in 2000 because we changed how they were to be coached halfway through their development. Of course the plan we setup in 2004 that will produce fruit in 2014 is obviously changed in 2008 when we also don't do very well and then SOMETHING MUST BE DONE, so we change our 2004 crop's methods. This obviously doesn't mean that we don't produce good players, it just means that we have no consistent style of football that we can identify as "English football"

This is what I see as the biggest trap that the USSF can fall into. I've been paying attention the the USMNT since Bob Bradley was appointed (who I thought was an excellent appointment) and over the years the US has began to play a very distinct style of football that is based on their culture to a degree. It's all about the hero mythology, the ultra-hard work, the acceptance of failure as part of any risk and the ability to look past it as well as an overwhelming enthusiasm tied with the physical dominance that is innate to their current sporting culture. At the moment at least to me the USSF has a style that it has fostered based upon the country and its ethics.

The problem is that as football in the US grows, more and more short term thinking will be happening amongst the media and the fanbase and more and more pressure to DO SOMETHING RIGHT NOW will be applied, which means that you'll end up copying the current flavour of the month. In 2000 that was the French, in 2004 that was the Spanish, in 2008 that was Greece and 2014 it was the Germans who all have very different ideas on how to play the game and their success is a fluke of timing and good planning. Following trends in football instead of attempting to predict them is the absolute death-knell for any national grassroot philosophy.

The USWNT's victory in the Women's World Cup is for the most part irrelevant to the conversation because women's football is globally underfunded and ignored, so not really a true measure of the game. The reasonable performance in 2014 and 2010 are more indicative, but again you have to consider that 3-5 games isn't truly representative of the performance of a national FA because it's such a short reference frame that silly things like an offside goal or a bad call can shape a result. This is why leagues are always more representative of quality than cups are and why they're harder to win.

With the above there's also really bad habits in the US mindset that just don't mix well with football. In most US sports there is a fascination with statistics and data that simply do not apply because the game is a chaotic system without controlled variables to compare against. In fact this is a really big thing that the US has wrong - not so much in the very small circumstances where data is useful but looking at things like shots per game or pass completion which are absolutely meaningless pieces of data that has no relevance to anything. The adherence to being a top athlete is great in one respect but also terrible in another as football is a mental rather than physical game. In the modern game you need to be a decent enough athlete to pull off the technique that you are trained on and that's about it - look at David Silva at City and compare him to Micah Richards. Richards was a six foot two stocky lad with 8% body fat naturally and was one of the quickest players on our team who could run for days. David Silva is a four foot nothing skinny lad who won't be breaking any squat records, doesn't have a great engine and is one of the slowest players on our team. He's also 500,000 times the footballer Richards is because he has a genius level brain and his technique is inch perfect. David Silva could never ever come through the current USSF system and it's only in the last 10 years that he could make it through England's
